publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems Engineering for Profit
abstract: Systems engineering has been developed as a convolution of organisation and individual engineering activity. Making a formal separation of concerns, it is argued that while systems engineering provides formal support and management of a platform, a position, a resource base for system engineering, system engineering is a composition of monitoring and modelling, defining and organising activities practised by individual engineers but with collective effect. These activities lead to the elaboration of systems and their support platforms with emergent properties meeting the requirements of customers which as projects become integrated into end-user environments. In the presentation, it is shown that system engineering is a response to business opportunity presented by differences in market demand and supply with the intention of reducing the so called quality-gap. The conclusion is that while system engineering is a profitless activity, profit can be associated, as an emergent property, with the systems engineering organisation. Such profit does not appear in financial terms, ostensibly, but as a reduction of outlay in the achievement of a given return, the delivery of the system to customers' satisfaction. Profit or loss making as a result of project management or engineering activity is argued to be a sign of poor system engineering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The role of different engineering methods
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems Engineering for Profit
abstract: Engineering has a pivotal role to play in the generation of profit in the increasingly uncertain world of manufacturing where many of the traditional functional roles are diminishing, or are being replaced by multifunctional teams as companies reorganise their business processes to react to increasing change, whether at the level of responding to small but rapid changes in market requirements, or at a more fundamental level of the adoption, or adaptation, of new technologies as companies undertake vigorous change in their efforts to remain in competitive positions. If manufacturing in Britain is to remain competitive into the 21st century it is necessary to understand what future cultural and organisational changes, and supporting technological changes, are going to be required and how the transition from the current state to an "Agile Manufacturing" state can be achieved throughout the industrial supply chain. Systems engineering has an important, evolving, role to play in the different engineering methods that we will see emerging in manufacturing industry as it changes to meet the global competition.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Overview of systems engineering with reference to the Channel Tunnel project
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems Engineering for Profit
abstract: There is a whole plethora of management advice on how businesses should be run or could be improved in order to achieve success. Indeed, so many different views have arisen that there is a fashionable side to this advice with different management theories in vogue from time to time. It is not the authors's intention simply to add another theory to an already overlong list. He aims to show how the fundamental principles of systems engineering already encapsulate all that is needed to undertake a successful new venture. With some references to the Channel Tunnel project, he proposes to give examples of how systems engineering both was and was not applied, with the consequent results.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Towards a guide to the practice of system engineering
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems Engineering for Profit
abstract: The author presents a draft guide to the practice of system engineering which is offered to system engineers as an aid to their professional practice and to organisations as an aid to system engineering management. The guide provides a definition of system engineering and states the aim, objectives an activities essential to good system engineering practice. Implicit in the guide is concern for improving quality, promoting integrity, managing risk and complexity, and providing the support for the needs and expectations of creating organisations, their engineers, customers and users. The guide is therefore an evolving standard against which projects and practices may be compared. A satisfactory comparison results when the spirit of each and every activity is satisfied. An unsatisfactory comparison results when any of the activities are not addressed or not addressed adequately.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Requirements for a practical engineering method for producing computer based systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems Engineering for Profit
abstract: South Bank University (SBU) teaches systems engineering in a computing context. They recognize that there are many different methods and that each is not suitable in all situations. Towards the end of the computing degree SBU tell students to view methods as tools in a tool box and that there is no one medicine for all ills. In developing this teaching the author is attempting to discover the criteria that might be considered important when selecting or designing a method(s) for constructing computer based systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Systems engineering and concurrent engineering: synonymous, complementary or contrary?
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Systems Engineering for Profit
abstract: Systems engineering emerged as the need to manage complexity in the development of large scale systems became pressing. Concurrent engineering was defined less than ten years ago and has commonly been adopted to address the need for development time scale reduction. Definitions of both systems engineering and concurrent engineering may lead an observer to conclude that they occupy the same territory and could even be synonymous. Textbooks and collections of papers under the two headings cover many of the same tools, perhaps confirming that observer's view. But a difference in the focus of systems engineering and concurrent engineering marks out their respective territories quite sharply. A less superficial observer might come to a realisation that a fully-empowered concurrent engineering team is unlikely to conform to the highly structured hierarchical systems engineering process that is proposed to engineer large systems. The two approaches appear quite contrary, instead. Both forms of engineering have the same objective in developing and introducing new products. Either their two domains (project size? technologies? market characteristics?) might be recognised and charted, or a synthesis might be attempted. The two approaches may be complementary.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
